name: Heinrich Bullinger
role: Swiss Reformer, Zwingli's successor as chief minister (Antistes) of the Zürich church

died.cause: Illness after months of decline in old age

summary: Leader of the Zürich church for over forty years after Zwingli's death, author of the Second Helvetic Confession and the Decades, and one of the most widely read and best-connected Reformed theologians of the sixteenth century.

key_dates.label: Studying at Cologne, turns to the Reformation through reading the Church Fathers and Luther
Becomes teacher at the Cistercian monastery school of Kappel
Succeeds his father as pastor of Bremgarten; marries Anna Adlischwyler, a former nun
Flees Bremgarten after the Catholic victory at Kappel (November); elected Zwingli's successor at Zürich (9 December)
Co-author of the First Helvetic Confession
Consensus Tigurinus with Calvin unites Zürich and Geneva on the Lord's Supper; the Decades begin to appear (1549–51)
Zürich's ministers, led by Bullinger, advise Geneva that Servetus should be punished; Servetus is burned (27 October)
Zürich takes in Protestant refugees expelled from Locarno
Second Helvetic Confession published, adopted by the Swiss Reformed churches and the Elector Palatine

accomplishments.text: Led the Zürich church as Antistes from 1531 until his death, steadying it after the defeat at Kappel and negotiating with the city council a settlement that kept the clergy's freedom to preach while limiting their role in politics.

Wrote the Second Helvetic Confession, first drafted as a personal statement of faith in 1561 and published in 1566; it became one of the most widely accepted Reformed confessions, adopted in Switzerland, Hungary, Poland, and elsewhere.
Agreed with Calvin the Consensus Tigurinus (1549), a common statement on the sacraments that drew the Zürich and Genevan churches together and marked the Reformed tradition off from the Lutheran.

Published the Decades (1549–51), fifty sermons on Christian doctrine; in English translation they were widely used in the Elizabethan church, and Archbishop John Whitgift ordered less-educated clergy to read them (1586).
Kept up a correspondence of about 12,000 surviving letters with reformers, rulers, and churches across Europe, and advised the churches of England, Hungary, and Poland.
Gave refuge and support to Protestant exiles, including English Protestants fleeing Mary I and the Protestants expelled from Locarno in 1555.
Developed an early theology of the covenant in On the One and Eternal Testament or Covenant of God (1534), influential in later Reformed covenant theology.

Wrote against the Anabaptists, including a history tracing them to the radicals of the 1520s (1560), and supported the Zürich council's use of fines, imprisonment, and banishment against them, defending the magistrate's right to punish obstinate heretics.
Endorsed the condemnation of Michael Servetus, advising Geneva in 1553 that he should be punished and approving his execution afterwards.
Wrote a history of the Reformation in the Swiss Confederation, an important if partisan source for Zwingli's career and death.

original.phrase: The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.
original.reference: Second Helvetic Confession (1566), chapter 1 (Praedicatio verbi Dei est verbum Dei)
original.note: A marginal heading in the confession, often quoted as a summary of the Reformed view of preaching.

persecution_note: Bullinger was never arrested, tried, or imprisoned. He and his father were driven from Bremgarten in 1531 when the Catholic cantons restored the Mass there after their victory at Kappel. As a leading Protestant his works were later placed on the Catholic Index. He was himself on the side of the authorities in the coercion of Anabaptists and in the case of Servetus, described among his accomplishments above.

persecution.title: Flight from Bremgarten
persecution.summary: After the Catholic cantons defeated Zürich at Kappel (11 October 1531), Bremgarten, in the jointly ruled Freie Ämter, was forced back to Catholicism. Bullinger, his father, and the Reformed party fled to Zürich.

responsible.name: The Five Catholic Cantons (Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug)
responsible.role: Victors at Kappel who imposed the restoration of Catholic worship

persecution.outcome: Exile to Zürich, where he was chosen to succeed Zwingli within weeks.

excommunication_note: No papal excommunication of Bullinger by name is recorded. As a Protestant minister he was outside the Catholic Church, and all his works were forbidden to Catholics.

excommunications.reason: Bullinger listed among authors all of whose works were forbidden to Catholics
